newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq denies massing troops on Kuwait border.
newsitem.headline: Iraq denies massing troops on Kuwait border.

text.p: Iraq denied on Saturday reports it was massing troops close to its southern border with Kuwait.
"A responsible military source denied the existence of any movements or reinforcements of Iraqi troops in southern Iraq," the Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
INA said the military source was responding to statements by Kuwait, which Iraq invaded in 1990 and a U.S.-led multinational force liberated in 1991, saying Baghdad was massing troops in the south.

"There are not any unusual reinforcements or movements at all or any change in the general plans adopted for daily training of our armed forces throughout Iraq, especially in the south," INA quoted the source as saying.

Kuwait's Information Minister Sheikh Saud Nasser al-Sabah was quoted by Kuwaiti newspapers on Saturday as saying Iraq had between 150,000 to 180,000 troops deployed some 50 km (30 miles) north of Kuwait.
In a statement to INA, Iraq's Culture and Information Minister Hamed Youssef Hummadi said al-Sabah's comments were immersed in "falsehood and fabrication".

"Mr Saud Nasser al-Sabah has no reputation for being the bearer of truth or keeping away from falsehood...he has an old history of lies and falsehood since he was (Kuwait's) ambassador of evil in Washington," Hummadi said.
White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said on Wednesday there were no indications of troop movements in Iraq that would suggest any renewed threat to Kuwait.

But he also said the United States saw signs of "struggles for power" going on in Iraq for control and that President Bill Clinton had "foremost on his mind the threats to regional security, particularly in the Persian Gulf".

The Iraqi military source said: "Those possessing the known surveillance means from satellites and other means have the ability to confirm this. Besides Iraq is not a closed country as the movement of people in it is known and is usual for Iraqis and non-Iraqis."

"There are a great deal of complicated internal struggles of power" going on in Iraq, McCurry told reporters when asked about a statement by a senior U.S. military official that Iraqi President Saddam Hussein had put his wife under house arrest.
British sources on Thursday said they did not see any sign of an impending crisis or any unusual military activity in Iraq despite "colourful" U.S. claims of a power struggle there.
"Things continue as normal. We have no heightened alert status," said one British offical on condition of anonymity.

Iraq's official press continued with its attack against the United States for a second day. "Fortunately, the vulgarity of the American imperialism and its criminal tendencies are known internationally," declared the government newspaper al-Jumhouriya in a front-page editorial.
The official al-Qadissiya said the current campaign against Iraq was part of the "Zionist, Atlantic and American aggression" launched against Iraq during the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.
Babel, the newspaper of Saddam's eldest son Uday. said the United States wanted to increase its pressure on Iraq and did not exclude all options among them "a military strike" by Washington.
